title: The Gift of the Magi
author: O. Henry (retold)
summary: お金のない若い夫婦が、クリスマスに互いへ贈り物をするため、それぞれの宝物を手放します。O・ヘンリーの名作をやや易しく。

source.note: Retold in simpler English from O. Henry’s “The Gift of the Magi” (1905, public domain).

paragraphs: One dollar and eighty-seven cents. That was all. Della counted it three times, and it was still one dollar and eighty-seven cents. And the next day would be Christmas.

Della and her husband, Jim, lived in a small, cheap apartment in New York. Jim earned twenty dollars a week, which was not much, and Della had been saving every penny she could for months. She had argued with the grocer and the butcher over every price, and still she had only one dollar and eighty-seven cents to buy a present for Jim.

She sat down on the old sofa and cried. Then she stood up, went to the window, and looked out at a gray cat walking along a gray fence in a gray backyard. She wanted to give Jim something fine, something worthy of him.

The couple owned two things that they were extremely proud of. One was Jim’s gold watch, which had belonged to his father and his grandfather before him. The other was Della’s hair. It was long, brown, and beautiful, falling below her knees like a shining waterfall.

Suddenly, Della turned from the window. Her eyes were bright, but her face had lost its color. She quickly let down her hair and looked at it in the mirror for a long moment. A tear or two fell on the old red carpet. Then she put on her old brown jacket and her old brown hat and hurried out into the street.
She stopped in front of a sign that read: “Madame Sofronie. Hair Goods of All Kinds.” Della ran up the stairs.

“Will you buy my hair?” she asked. “I buy hair,” said Madame. “Take your hat off and let me look at it.” Down fell the brown waterfall. “Twenty dollars,” said Madame, lifting it with an expert hand. “Give it to me quickly,” said Della.

For the next two hours, Della searched the shops for Jim’s present. At last she found it: a simple platinum chain for his watch. Jim’s watch was beautiful, but because he had only an old leather strap, he sometimes looked at it secretly, almost ashamed. With this chain, he could check the time proudly in any company. It cost twenty-one dollars, and she hurried home with the eighty-seven cents that was left.

At home, she used her curling irons to fix what was left of her hair. When she finished, her head was covered with tiny, close curls, and she looked like a schoolboy. “If Jim doesn’t kill me,” she said to herself, “he’ll say I look like a chorus girl. But what could I do with a dollar and eighty-seven cents?”

At seven o’clock, the coffee was ready and the pan was hot for cooking the meat. Della heard Jim’s step on the stairs, and she turned white for a moment. “Please, God,” she whispered, “make him think I am still pretty.”

The door opened, and Jim stepped in. He looked thin and very serious. He was only twenty-two, and he needed a new coat and gloves. He stopped inside the door and stared at Della. There was an expression in his eyes that she could not read. It was not anger, nor surprise, nor any of the feelings she had prepared for. He simply stared at her.

“Jim, darling,” she cried, “don’t look at me that way. I had my hair cut off and sold it because I couldn’t live through Christmas without giving you a present. It’ll grow out again. My hair grows awfully fast. Say ‘Merry Christmas,’ Jim, and let’s be happy.”
“You’ve cut off your hair?” Jim asked slowly, as if he could not understand it even after thinking hard.

Then he seemed to wake up. He took a package from his coat pocket and threw it on the table. “Don’t make any mistake, Dell,” he said. “Nothing like a haircut could make me love you any less. But if you open that package, you’ll see why I was so surprised.”

Della opened it. Inside were the combs: a set of beautiful combs, made of real tortoise shell with jeweled edges, that she had admired for a long time in a shop window on Broadway. They were exactly the right color for her lost hair. She had wanted them without any hope of owning them. And now they were hers, but the hair that should have worn them was gone.

She held them close, and at last she was able to look up with a smile and say, “My hair grows so fast, Jim!” Then she remembered his present. She held out the chain to him eagerly on her open hand. “Isn’t it wonderful, Jim? I searched all over town to find it. Give me your watch. I want to see how it looks on it.”

Instead of obeying, Jim sat down on the sofa, put his hands behind his head, and smiled. “Dell,” he said, “let’s put our Christmas presents away and keep them for a while. They’re too nice to use just now. I sold the watch to get the money to buy your combs. And now, suppose you start cooking the meat.”

The Magi, as you know, were wise men who brought gifts to the baby in the manger. They invented the art of giving Christmas presents. This has been the story of two foolish young people who unwisely gave up the greatest treasures of their house for each other. But of all who give gifts, these two were the wisest. They are the Magi.
